title: The Bitcoin Auction
creator: Bitcoin
deck: An asset seized from an online marketplace entered a government sale.
story: A gavel waits beside a stack of envelopes. Warm light falls across a locked box, a book and an auction sheet. Everything in the room suggests paperwork, custody and procedure, yet the asset being sold cannot be lifted onto the desk. LORE gives the sale of digital money the weight of a traditional auction, using familiar objects to picture an unfamiliar government lot.

On 27 June 2014, the US Marshals Service held an online auction for approximately 29,656 BTC forfeited from wallet files on Silk Road’s servers. The sale followed the marketplace’s shutdown in 2013. It covered this specific group of bitcoins, rather than every coin seized in the wider investigation; the separate, much larger holding seized from Ross Ulbricht was excluded from the June sale.

Registered participants submitted bids electronically during a twelve-hour window. The sealed-bid process asked them to state their offers without an open room of rivals calling out prices. The bitcoins were divided into ten lots, and venture capitalist Tim Draper was subsequently identified as the buyer of the entire offering. The physical envelopes and gavel in the illustration give that process a shape, but do not reconstruct its actual operation.

The contrast is what makes the moment memorable. Money associated with a hidden online market was passing through a public institution’s formal disposal process. The asset remained digital; the authority controlling its next transfer had changed. LORE leaves the buyer outside the frame and keeps attention on the handover itself. A library slip quietly leads back to Silk Road’s earlier chapter, while the dated sheet brings the story forward to the sale.

details.title: A book and a library slip
details.text: The navy Princess Bride book and cream-and-red Glen Park slip return from 016, Silk Road Shutdown. They connect the chapters visually, without claiming those objects appeared at the auction.

details.title: The evidence cord
details.text: Red cord and a blank tag sit with the locked box. They symbolise an asset moving from seizure into disposal, not destroyed evidence or a box holding physical bitcoins.

details.title: Envelopes and a gavel
details.text: These familiar auction objects stand for formal bidding. The June sale was conducted online with sealed bids; the room and its desk are an illustrative interpretation, not a documentary reconstruction.

details.title: The dated sheet
details.text: BITCOIN and JUNE 2014 anchor the paperwork to this sale. The final illustration does not print the quantity of bitcoins; the approximately 29,656 BTC figure belongs to the historical account.

source_art_note: The [FBI’s retrospective](https://leb.fbi.gov/articles/featured-articles/virtual-currency-investigative-challenges-and-opportunities) records the June sale and amount; [ABC News](https://abcnews.com/blogs/headlines/2014/06/bitcoin-bonanza-us-marshals-auction-nearly-18m-worth-of-net-currency) documents its date and scope. [Contemporary Reuters reporting](https://uk.sports.yahoo.com/news/exclusive-venture-capitalist-draper-wins-u-marshals-bitcoin-124950853--sector.html) identifies the online sealed-bid format and buyer, while the [archived lot record](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/USMS_June_2014_auction) lists ten lots. The official’s identity, room, envelopes, gavel and callback objects are imagined. FROM SEIZURE TO SALE is editorial copy; no physical coin hoard or live auction-room scene is claimed.
